items.name: risk, control and evidence
rd: An IT application control is a control built into the system that runs automatically every time a transaction is processed, so it does not depend on a person remembering to do it.

Two SAP examples: the three-way match in purchasing and invoice verification, where SAP blocks an invoice for payment if price or quantity differ from the purchase order and goods receipt beyond a set tolerance; and posting period control, where configuration in OB52 stops users from posting to closed periods.
The key differences from manual controls are consistency and testing approach. A manual control can fail on any day, so we test a sample across the year.

An automated control behaves the same way every time, so if the ITGCs over change management and access are effective, I can test it once per scenario and then confirm the configuration did not change during the period. If the ITGCs are weak, that assumption falls away and I need much more testing.
I would expect controls in four places. At the source, the payroll results are approved before they are sent.
In transit, control totals such as record count and total amount are sent with the file and checked by SAP on receipt, and the file is protected from changes.
On receipt, interface errors are logged and monitored, for example in the interface or IDoc monitoring, and every error is fixed and reprocessed.
And afterwards, a reconciliation between the payroll register and what posted in the SAP ledger, reviewed and signed by someone in finance.
To test, I walk through one payroll run end to end, then test a sample of runs: control totals agreed, errors resolved, and the reconciliation done on time with differences explained.
I also check who can change the interface mapping or the batch job, because that is a change management and access risk, and I consider whether the payroll provider's SOC 1 covers the source side.
The ITGC domains in an SAP landscape
I group SAP ITGCs into three domains.

First, access to programs and data: user provisioning, leavers, periodic access reviews, privileged access such as SAP_ALL or firefighter IDs, and password and system parameter settings. If access is weak, someone could post or change financial data without authority.

Second, program change: changes move from development to quality to production through transports, with approval, testing and segregation between developers and the people who import into production. If change is weak, a configuration or code change could break an automated control without anyone noticing.
Third, IT operations: batch job scheduling and monitoring in SM37, interface monitoring, and backup and recovery. If operations fail, transactions can be missed or duplicated.
Some firms add a fourth domain, program development, for new implementations.

The reason all of this matters is reliance: the external auditor relies on automated controls and system-generated reports, and that reliance is only valid if the ITGCs around them operated effectively for the whole period.
al: A control is a safeguard that reduces the likelihood or the impact of something going wrong. A preventive control stops the problem happening; a detective control finds it after it has happened.
Evidence must show that the control operated. A policy only describes the control; it does not show the control was performed. “Approval is required” is not evidence of approvals.
For a payment sent twice, the best evidence is the payment log for both runs, the bank or clearing record, and the reversal or supplier credit.

qs.x: A control is best defined as:
o: A safeguard that reduces the likelihood or the impact of something going wrong
Evidence that a transaction took place
A report that lists all exceptions found during testing
A policy document approved by the board
qs.e: A control is the safeguard. Evidence is what you inspect to decide whether the safeguard worked. Policies and reports can support a control but are not the control itself.

qs.x: Which pair correctly matches the control type to what it does?
o: Preventive stops the problem happening; detective finds it after it has happened
Preventive finds the problem after it has happened; detective stops it
Preventive restores the system; detective approves the change
Preventive is always manual; detective is always automated
qs.e: Preventive controls act before the event (for example a closed posting period). Detective controls find it during or after (for example a monthly review of SAP_ALL users). Corrective controls limit damage and restore.

qs.x: A company orders three laptops and receives two. The invoice is for three. Which control prevents payment for the missing laptop?
o: A rule that blocks the invoice when invoiced quantity exceeds the goods received
A quarterly access review of the buyers
A daily backup of the purchasing tables
A policy that says buyers must be honest
qs.e: The three-way match compares the order, the receipt and the invoice. It is a preventive application control. The other options address access, availability or intent, not the quantity difference.

qs.x: A payment was sent to a supplier twice. Which evidence best shows whether the second payment was detected and resolved?
o: The payment log for both runs, the bank or clearing record and the reversal or supplier credit
The user list of the accounts payable team
qs.e: You need to see both payments, what happened at the bank and how it was corrected. A single invoice or a policy does not show detection or resolution.

qs.x: A reviewer’s note says: “Control is effective because the policy requires an approval.” What is the main weakness?
o: A policy describes the control; it does not show the control operated
The note should name the reviewer
qs.e: A policy or narrative is a description, not proof. Until you have seen real evidence of the control operating, you have tested a description, not a control.

items.name: SOX and COSO
rd: Section 302 requires the CEO and CFO of a US-listed company to personally certify each quarterly and annual report, including that they are responsible for internal controls and have disclosed significant deficiencies and material weaknesses.

Section 404 has two parts: 404(a) requires management to assess and report on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting each year, and 404(b) requires the external auditor of larger companies to give its own opinion on those controls.

IT controls fit in because almost every financial process runs through systems like SAP. Automated controls and system reports are only reliable if the IT general controls around them work, so ITGCs and application controls are tested as part of the 404 programme.
In practice, my testing either supports management's assessment or is used, or re-performed, by the external auditor, which is why the evidence and documentation have to stand up to scrutiny.

COSO 2013 is the framework most US companies use for internal control over financial reporting. It has five components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities, supported by 17 principles.

For an IT controls consultant, the most direct link is control activities, and in particular principle 11, which says the organization selects and develops general control activities over technology, which is where ITGCs sit.
But the others matter too. Risk assessment drives which systems are in scope.
Information and communication covers the quality of information used in controls, which is where testing the completeness and accuracy of system reports comes in.
And monitoring covers ongoing and separate evaluations, such as access reviews and control self-assessments.
When a deficiency is evaluated, the auditor also considers the control environment, for example whether management overrides controls.

qs.x: Section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires:
o: The CEO and CFO to certify each periodic report and their responsibility for controls
Management to hire an external auditor
The external auditor to test every control
The board to approve each journal entry
qs.e: 302 is personal certification by the CEO and CFO of each quarterly and annual report, including disclosure of significant deficiencies and material weaknesses.

qs.x: Section 404 has two parts. Which statement is correct?
o: 404(a) requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting; 404(b) requires the external auditor of larger companies to give an opinion
404(a) is the auditor’s opinion; 404(b) is management’s certification
404(a) covers IT only; 404(b) covers finance only
404(a) applies to quarterly reports only; 404(b) to annual reports only
qs.e: Management assesses and reports under 404(a). The external auditor gives its own opinion on controls under 404(b), for larger companies.

qs.x: How many components and principles does the COSO 2013 framework have?
qs.e: The five components are control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring, supported by 17 principles.

qs.x: Which COSO principle is the direct link to IT general controls?
o: Principle 11: general control activities over technology
qs.e: Principle 11 says the organisation selects and develops general control activities over technology. That is where ITGCs sit.

qs.x: A tester checks that the report used for a monthly review is complete and accurate. Which COSO component does this mainly relate to?
qs.e: Information and communication covers the quality of information used in controls, which is why testing the completeness and accuracy of system reports matters.

items.name: COBIT, three lines and standards
rd: COSO is a general framework for internal control, used by most companies to assess internal control over financial reporting under SOX.

COBIT, from ISACA, is a framework for the governance and management of enterprise IT. It covers far more than financial reporting, including IT strategy, risk, security, service delivery and performance measurement.

In SOX work, COSO is the framework management reports against, and COBIT is often used underneath it to organise and describe the IT general controls, for example mapping access, change and operations controls to COBIT processes, or using its maturity approach in advisory work.

I would use COBIT when a client wants to improve IT governance more broadly, or when designing an ITGC framework from scratch, while keeping the SOX conclusion tied to COSO and the financial reporting risks.
Lines of defence and who does what
The Three Lines model separates responsibilities. The first line is management and the control owners who run the business and operate the controls.
The second line is functions such as risk management, compliance and often the SOX programme office, which set frameworks and monitor.
The third line is internal audit, which gives independent assurance to the board.
The external auditor sits outside the organisation and gives its own opinion.

As a controls consultant, where I sit depends on the engagement: helping the SOX office design and test controls puts me in a second-line role, while supporting internal audit testing puts me in a third-line role.

Either way I work closely with the external auditor: I agree the plan, sample sizes and evidence standards at the start, so they can rely on our testing where allowed. I also guard independence, for example I do not test controls I designed, and I do not operate controls on the client's behalf.
Top-down, risk-based means starting from the financial statements, not from the system. First I identify significant accounts and disclosures, using materiality and qualitative risk.
Then the relevant assertions for each, such as existence or completeness, and the processes and transactions that feed them.
Then the risks of material misstatement in those processes, and the key controls that address them, choosing the most efficient mix of manual and automated controls.

Only then do I look at technology: which systems support those key controls or produce the reports they rely on. Those systems, such as the SAP production client for finance and logistics, and the database and operating system beneath it, are in scope for ITGCs.

This approach is what PCAOB AS 2201 expects of the external auditor, and following it means we test what matters and can defend why other areas are out of scope. I document each step so the scope can be challenged and explained.
al: Independence: do not test a control you designed. Raise it with your lead, because your objectivity is compromised.

qs.x: Which statement about COBIT and COSO is most accurate?
o: COSO is the framework management reports against; COBIT is often used underneath to organise IT controls
COSO covers IT governance; COBIT covers only financial statements
They are the same framework with different names
qs.e: COSO is the internal control framework most US companies report against. COBIT covers governance and management of enterprise IT and is used to describe and organise the ITGCs.

qs.x: In the Three Lines model, who sits in the first line?
o: Management and control owners who operate the controls
qs.e: The first line runs the business and operates controls. The second line sets frameworks and monitors (risk, compliance, often the SOX office). The third line is internal audit. The external auditor is outside the model.

qs.x: A consultant helps the client’s SOX office design and test controls. Which line does the work fall in?
qs.e: Helping the SOX office design and test controls is a second-line role. Supporting internal audit testing would be a third-line role.

qs.x: You are asked to test a control that you helped design last quarter. What is the right response?
o: Raise it with your lead: you should not test controls you designed, because independence is compromised
Test it anyway because you know it best
Test it but skip the design walkthrough
Ask the control owner to sign the workpaper
qs.e: Guarding independence is part of the role: do not test controls you designed and do not operate controls on the client’s behalf.

qs.x: The PCAOB standard that expects a top-down, risk-based approach to the audit of internal control is:
qs.e: AS 2201 sets out the top-down, risk-based approach. Starting from the financial statements keeps testing on what matters and lets you defend why other areas are out of scope.

items.name: ITGC domains and the 12-phase map
rd: The ITGC domains in an SAP landscape
I group SAP ITGCs into three domains.

First, access to programs and data: user provisioning, leavers, periodic access reviews, privileged access such as SAP_ALL or firefighter IDs, and password and system parameter settings. If access is weak, someone could post or change financial data without authority.

Second, program change: changes move from development to quality to production through transports, with approval, testing and segregation between developers and the people who import into production. If change is weak, a configuration or code change could break an automated control without anyone noticing.
Third, IT operations: batch job scheduling and monitoring in SM37, interface monitoring, and backup and recovery. If operations fail, transactions can be missed or duplicated.
Some firms add a fourth domain, program development, for new implementations.

The reason all of this matters is reliance: the external auditor relies on automated controls and system-generated reports, and that reliance is only valid if the ITGCs around them operated effectively for the whole period.
al: The 12 phases: 0 Onboarding and mobilisation; 1 Planning and scoping; 2 Understanding the controls and the RCM; 3 Test planning; 4 Evidence extraction and IPE (get populations from SAP and prove them complete and accurate); 5 Interim testing: access; 6 Interim testing: change, operations, SDLC; 7 Relying on the SOC 1 report; 8 Exceptions, deficiencies and findings; 9 Remediation and retesting; 10 Roll-forward and year-end testing; 11 Review, reporting and close-out.
Phase 0 rookie mistake: waiting until week three to request access, or assuming last year’s file shows this year. Lost access time is never recovered, and last year’s populations miss what changed.

qs.x: The three ITGC domains most commonly tested in an SAP landscape are:
o: Access to programs and data, program change, and IT operations
qs.e: Many firms add a fourth domain, program development, for new implementations. Confidentiality, integrity and availability describe security properties, not the ITGC domains.

qs.x: A batch job that posts payments fails and nobody notices. Which ITGC domain failed?
qs.e: Batch job scheduling and monitoring belongs to IT operations. If operations fail, transactions can be missed or duplicated.

qs.x: Why do auditors care whether ITGCs worked?
o: Because reliance on automated controls and system reports is only valid if the ITGCs operated for the whole period
Because SOX requires an IT audit every month
qs.e: Weak ITGCs undermine every automated control and report that depends on them.

qs.x: In the 12-phase Thornfield project, which phase is where you take populations from SAP and prove them complete and accurate?
qs.e: Phase 4 is evidence extraction and information produced by the entity (IPE). Phase 1 is scoping; Phase 8 evaluates exceptions; Phase 10 covers the remaining period.

qs.x: Which is a rookie mistake that can invalidate Phase 0 (mobilisation)?
o: Waiting until week three to request access, or assuming last year’s file shows this year
qs.e: Testers who wait to request access lose a week they never get back, and copying last year’s populations misses everything that changed.

items.name: design and operating effectiveness
rd: Design is whether the control, if it works as described, would prevent or detect the risk.
Operating effectiveness is whether it actually worked consistently throughout the period.

I test design first, usually with a walkthrough: I follow one transaction end to end, inspect the evidence and confirm the control addresses the risk at the right precision. For example, for a vendor bank change review, I check that the review covers all bank changes, is done by someone independent, and happens before the payment run.
Then I test operating effectiveness with a sample over the period, for example two quarters of the review if it is quarterly, or 25 instances if it happens several times a day.
If the design fails, there is no point testing operation; I raise it as a design deficiency with my lead straight away, because it means the risk is not covered at all.
al: Testing a setting: a screenshot proves only one moment. To cover the period you need change logs or change documents for the whole year.

qs.x: Design effectiveness asks:
o: Whether the control, if operated as described, would prevent or detect the risk
Whether the control worked every day of the year
Whether the control owner is competent
qs.e: Design is about whether the control would work if performed as described. Operating effectiveness is whether it actually worked consistently throughout the period.

qs.x: A quarterly review is tested for operating effectiveness. A common sample is:
o: Every review for the last five years
qs.e: The sample follows how often the control runs. Quarterly: typically two. A control that runs several times a day: typically 25 or more.

qs.x: A control fails the design test: it does not cover all bank changes. What do you do?
o: Raise it as a design deficiency with your lead straight away; there is no point testing operation
Test operation anyway and average the result
Ask the owner to reword the control description
qs.e: If the design fails the risk is not covered at all. Testing how consistently a flawed control operated adds little, and delay costs time to fix.

qs.x: For a vendor bank change review, which design check is most important?
o: That the review covers all bank changes, is performed by someone independent and happens before the payment run
That the reviewer has the longest tenure
That the review is on the first day of the month
That the evidence is in colour
qs.e: Design must match the risk: complete coverage, independence and timing before the payment can be made.

qs.x: Which statement shows a good understanding of testing the current setting?
o: A screenshot of a configuration proves only one moment; to test the period you need change logs for the whole year
A screenshot proves the whole year if it is dated
The current setting is enough if the ITGCs are tested next year
qs.e: Controls over settings are tested through change logs across the period, not today’s screen.

items.name: Week 1 review (with spaced questions)
items.note: No new reading. Re-read this week’s Monday to Friday reading boxes, and the boxes of the earlier weeks this review draws on, before you start.

qs.x: Where do IT controls fit into SOX 404?
o: Automated controls and reports are only reliable if the ITGCs work, so ITGCs and application controls are tested in the 404 programme
They do not; 404 is about finance only
They are required only for non-US companies
qs.e: Almost every financial process runs on systems. The reliance chain runs from financial statements to automated controls to ITGCs.

qs.x: A population for a control test is taken from the ticket system. What risk does this create?
o: Users or changes that bypassed the ticket can never appear in the population
The sample will be too large
The tickets will be out of date
The auditor will reject electronic tickets
qs.e: A population from the place the control is recorded cannot show what bypassed it, and those are the cases you are testing for.

qs.x: A colleague says “COSO covers only finance, so IT is irrelevant to COSO.” Best reply?
o: Principle 11 covers general control activities over technology, so IT is directly in scope
Agree, IT belongs to COBIT only
COSO and IT are only linked in the control environment
COSO does not mention IT at all
qs.e: Principle 11 links COSO to ITGCs. COBIT is often used underneath to organise them.

qs.x: You test a daily automated control with one sample, after confirming the ITGCs are effective. Why is one sample often enough?
o: An automated control behaves the same way every time, provided the configuration did not change and ITGCs are effective
The auditor never checks automated controls
Daily controls always need one sample
qs.e: If the ITGCs are weak, the assumption falls away and you need much more testing.

qs.x: The 12 phases of the Thornfield project run from Phase 0 to:
qs.e: Phase 0 is onboarding and mobilisation; Phase 11 is review, reporting and close-out.

qs.x: A firm asks you to write the control, test it and sign it off yourself. Which principle is breached?
o: Independence: you do not test controls you designed
Segregation of duties in the SAP ruleset
qs.e: Independence requires separation between designing or operating a control and testing it.

items.name: testing user provisioning
rd: I start by getting the population from SAP itself: all users created, and all role assignments added, during the period. I use the user master data in USR02 for creation dates and the change documents for role assignments, run through SUIM or the GRC reports, and I record the parameters and run date so the population can be re-created. I check completeness by comparing the count with a second view of the same data.
Then I select a sample using our sampling guidance, typically 25 for a control that happens many times a day.

For each sample I trace back to the access request: was there a request, was it approved by the right person, was the approval before the access was granted, and does the access actually given match what was approved. If GRC Access Request Management is used, I also check that the risk analysis was run and any conflicts were mitigated before approval.
I document each sample with screenshots or exports, and I conclude on design and operating effectiveness. Any sample that fails becomes an exception that I evaluate, not one I explain away.
al: If a population does not agree to another source (for example 131 users created against 120 requests), treat the difference as unexplained: find who created each user and why, and do not sample until it is explained.

qs.x: Where should the population for a provisioning test come from?
o: SAP itself: user master data and the change documents for role assignments
qs.e: Take the population from the place the risk happens, not the place the control is recorded. Tickets cannot show access that bypassed them.

qs.x: Which table holds user creation data that you can use to build the population of users created in the period?
qs.e: USR02 holds user master logon data including creation dates. SM37 is job overview, SCC4 is client settings and STMS is transport management.

qs.x: For each sampled user, which question do you ask first when tracing to the access request?
o: Was there a request, approved by the right person, before the access was granted, and does the access given match what was approved?
Who is the user’s manager’s manager?
Is the role name spelt correctly?
qs.e: The test is request, right approver, timing before access, and a match between what was approved and what was given.

qs.x: The approval email for a sampled user is dated two days after the access was granted. How do you record it?
o: As an exception to a control that requires approval before access is given; then evaluate
As a pass because an approval exists
As a pass if the approver is senior
qs.e: A later approval is a factual difference from the control. Evaluate it; do not explain it away. If an emergency path allows retrospective approval, check the criteria and time limit first.

qs.x: The ticket tool lists 120 access requests. USR02 shows 131 users created in the same period. What is the right next step?
o: Treat the 11 users as unexplained, find who created each and why, and do not sample until the gap is explained
Sample from the 131 and ignore the gap
Ask the control owner to delete the 11 users
qs.e: The 11 may be service accounts or interface-created users, or real unauthorised access. Explain them first and raise genuine cases with your lead the same day.

items.name: leavers and terminations
rd: Automated or not, I test it. I get a list of everyone who left during the period from the HR system, and I check that the list itself is complete, for example by agreeing headcount movements.
I then compare it with SAP: for each leaver, when was the user locked or the validity date ended, and was that within the client's policy, often one or three business days.
Because the process is automated, I also look at the automated part as an application control: how the HR interface triggers the lock, and whether that configuration changed during the year.

For any leaver whose access stayed open too long, I check the last logon date and the change documents to see whether the account was used after the leave date. Late removal with no use is still an exception, but a much lower risk than late removal with activity.
I also look for accounts not linked to HR at all, such as contractors and generic IDs, because the automated process usually does not cover them.
al: A leaver you cannot find in SAP is a pass only after you have checked the other ways the user might appear: alias, name and personnel number.

qs.x: What must you prove before you compare the HR leavers list to SAP?
o: That the HR leavers list itself is complete (who produced it, from what, with which parameters)
That every leaver has a manager
That SAP has a leavers table
qs.e: If the HR list is incomplete, the test is about the wrong population. Agree headcount movements as a completeness check.

qs.x: HR says the leaver process is fully automated. Which additional test is needed?
o: Test the interface that triggers the lock as an application control, including whether its configuration changed during the year
None; automation removes the need to test
qs.e: Automated or not, you test it. The automated part is an application control, which depends on ITGCs and unchanged configuration.

qs.x: A leaver was locked five business days after the leave date against a three-day policy. There is no logon after the leave date. How do you treat it?
o: An exception to the control, but a lower risk than late removal with activity; evaluate and document
Not an exception because no logon occurred
Ignore it because it was only two days late
qs.e: Late removal with no use is still an exception, but the risk is much lower than late removal with activity. Check the last logon date and change documents.

qs.x: Which accounts does an HR-triggered process usually miss?
o: Contractors, generic and service IDs not linked to HR
qs.e: Look for accounts not linked to HR at all, because the automated process does not cover them.

qs.x: The 18 leavers in the HR list show 16 locked on time. One cannot be found in SAP. What do you do?
o: Confirm they never had access (alias, name, personnel number) before treating it as a pass
Treat it as a pass because no account exists
qs.e: Absence of an account is only informative if you have checked the other ways the user might appear in the system.

items.name: privileged and emergency access
rd: First I confirm the facts: which users, whether the profile is active and valid, when it was assigned and by whom, using SUIM and the user change documents. I separate expected cases, such as an emergency firefighter ID locked by default, from real issues, such as named dialog users who hold SAP_ALL permanently. For any real issue I find out the business reason and who approved it.

Then I look at what those users actually did: the security audit log in SM20 if it is active, and change documents for sensitive tables and master data. If I cannot show what was done, that gap is itself a problem.
I raise it with my lead the same day, because permanent SAP_ALL in production undermines both access and change controls, and it may affect reliance on other controls.
The usual remediation is to remove the profile, move genuine emergency needs to a firefighter process with logging and review, and assess whether the access was misused during the period.

Emergency access gives temporary, powerful access for urgent fixes, so it needs strong controls around it. In GRC Emergency Access Management, users request a firefighter ID with a reason; the session is logged, including transactions run and changes made; and a controller, who is independent of the user, reviews the log within an agreed time, often a few days.
To test it, I get the population of all firefighter sessions in the period from GRC, check it is complete against the firefighter log reports, and select a sample.

For each one I check there was a valid reason linked to a ticket, that the activity matched the reason, that the controller reviewed and signed off on time, and that anything unexpected was followed up.
I also check who is assigned as owner and controller, that controllers are not reviewing themselves, and who can use firefighter IDs at all.

qs.x: SUIM shows five users with SAP_ALL in production. What do you do first?
o: Confirm the facts: which users, active or locked, assigned when and by whom; separate expected cases from real issues
Remove the profile from all five immediately
Ask the users to explain by email
qs.e: Facts first. A firefighter ID locked by default is expected; named dialog users with permanent SAP_ALL are a real issue. Then business reason and approval.

qs.x: You need to see what the users with SAP_ALL actually did. Which sources do you use?
o: The security audit log (SM20) if active, and change documents for sensitive tables and master data
qs.e: If you cannot show what was done, that gap is itself a problem.

qs.x: In GRC Emergency Access Management, who reviews the firefighter session log?
o: A controller who is independent of the user
The user who ran the session
The Basis administrator who owns the system
qs.e: The review must be by someone independent, within an agreed time. A controller reviewing themselves defeats the control.

qs.x: For each sampled firefighter session you check:
o: A valid reason linked to a ticket, that activity matched the reason, and that the controller reviewed on time and followed up anything unexpected
That the user changed their password
That the session lasted exactly one hour
That the ticket has an attachment
qs.e: Reason, activity, timely independent review and follow-up are the four checks.

qs.x: The population of firefighter sessions came from the controller’s own spreadsheet. What do you do?
o: Get the population from GRC and check it is complete against the firefighter log reports
Accept it because the controller prepared it
qs.e: A population supplied by the control owner is information produced by the entity; prove it complete and accurate before use.

items.name: access reviews, SoD and mitigating controls
rd: User access reviews that actually work
An access review works when the right person reviews a complete and understandable list and the changes they ask for actually happen. Auditors fail reviews for four common reasons.
The list was incomplete, for example missing service accounts or a second system, so I compare the list given to reviewers with a system extract from the same date.
The reviewer could not understand it, for example role names with no description, so they approved everything; I look for evidence of real review, such as some removals or questions.
The review was late or not signed off.
And requested removals were never processed, so I trace a sample of removals to SAP change documents.

A good design also covers privileged and firefighter access separately, and has the reviewer be someone who knows the job, usually the line manager or role owner, not the security team reviewing their own work.
I accept the business reason as a starting point, then test the mitigation like any other control.

First, does it actually address the specific risk? A general monthly review of expenses does not mitigate the risk of changing vendor bank details and paying them; a review of all vendor bank changes before each payment run does.
Second, is it performed by someone independent of the user with the conflict?
Third, is it precise enough and frequent enough to catch the problem in time?
Fourth, is there evidence that it happened, every period, for the whole year?
In GRC I also check that the mitigating control is assigned to that user and risk, with a valid date range and an owner, and that monitors are notified.

If all of that holds, the conflict is accepted as mitigated and documented. If not, the options are to remove the access, split the role, or design a proper mitigation, and the business owner signs off on whichever is chosen.
Segregation of duties means no single person should be able to start, approve and hide a transaction on their own, because that creates the chance for fraud or error without anyone noticing.

A classic SAP example is in purchase to pay: if one user can create or change a vendor master record, for example in transaction XK02 or the business partner transaction, and can also run the payment program in F110, they could change a vendor's bank details to their own account and pay it.
In SAP GRC Access Control this shows up as a risk in the ruleset, made of two functions, vendor maintenance and payment processing, each with their actions and permissions.
When I find a conflict I look at whether it is real, whether the access is used, and whether there is a mitigating control, such as a review of vendor bank changes before each payment run.

qs.x: Which pair of functions is the classic SoD conflict in purchase to pay?
o: Vendor master maintenance and payment processing
qs.e: One person who can change vendor bank details and run the payment program could pay themselves. In GRC it appears as a risk made of two functions.

qs.x: Which is a common reason auditors fail a periodic user access review?
o: The list reviewers received was incomplete, for example missing service accounts or a second system
The review was done on a Tuesday
The list was in alphabetical order
qs.e: Others are: the reviewer could not understand the list, the review was late or unsigned, and removals were never processed.

qs.x: How do you check that requested removals were actually carried out?
o: Trace a sample of removals to SAP change documents
Check the ticket status is Closed
qs.e: A Closed ticket does not remove a role. Check the system.

qs.x: The business wants to keep a conflicting role and says a monthly expense review mitigates it. Is that valid?
o: No: a general expense review does not address the specific risk, so test fit, independence, precision, evidence and GRC assignment
Yes: any review mitigates any conflict
Yes if the reviewer is senior
Yes if the review exists on paper
qs.e: The mitigation must cover the specific risk. A review of all vendor bank changes before each payment run does; a general expense review does not.

qs.x: The reviewer approves 100% of items in a few minutes every month. What do you conclude?
o: The control may not be operating; real review would show questions or removals
qs.e: Speed and 100% approval suggest the reviewer did not actually review. Look for evidence of real review.

items.name: GRC risk analysis, role design, database access
rd: How access risk analysis works in GRC

GRC compares each user's or role's authorizations against a ruleset. The ruleset defines risks; each risk is a combination of functions, each function is a set of actions such as transaction codes, and each action can be refined with permission values, such as an authorization object and activity.
Analysis can run at action level, which is broader, or at permission level, which is more precise and reduces false positives.
For results to be reliable, three things must be true. The ruleset must be complete and approved, and changes to it must go through change control, because deleting a risk makes conflicts disappear.
The repository and authorization sync jobs must have run successfully, otherwise GRC is analysing old data.
And the analysis must cover all relevant systems and users, including firefighter IDs and service accounts.
When I test, I check all three before I rely on any report, and I re-run analysis for a sample of users to confirm the output.

Someone with powerful access to the HANA database can read or change tables directly, without going through SAP's application controls, authorizations or change documents. That can undermine every control above it. So I test four things.
Who has database accounts, and whether each is justified and approved, taking the user list from the database itself.
Who holds powerful system privileges, such as user administration or the ability to change data in the SAP schema, and whether the default SYSTEM user is deactivated or tightly controlled.
Whether audit policies are switched on for privileged activity, such as changes to users and privileges and direct data changes. And whether someone independent reviews those audit logs.
If the client is on RISE, much of the database administration is done by SAP, so I check the SOC 1 for those controls and focus my own testing on any database access the client keeps.
I would not start by working user by user. First I make sure the numbers are real: confirm the ruleset is right for the client and run permission-level analysis to remove false positives.
Then I analyse at role level, because most user conflicts come from a few badly designed roles; fixing one role can clear dozens of conflicts.
Next I use usage data to remove access people have not used, which is quick and low-risk.

What is left needs business decisions: redesign or split roles, reassign duties, or accept the risk with a tested mitigating control, signed off by the business owner. I prioritize by risk, starting with the critical financial risks like vendor payments and journal posting.

To keep it clean, I make sure risk analysis runs before access is approved in access requests, and that new roles are checked in Business Role Management before they go live. I report progress weekly with a simple measure: open critical conflicts by owner.

qs.x: In a GRC ruleset, a risk is made up of:
o: Two or more functions, each a set of actions (transaction codes) that can be refined with permission values
qs.e: Risks combine functions; functions are sets of actions; actions can be refined with permissions.

qs.x: Why does running access risk analysis at permission level reduce false positives?
o: It checks the authorization values, not only whether a transaction code is present
qs.e: Action-level analysis is broader; permission-level is more precise.

qs.x: What three things make GRC risk analysis results reliable?
o: An approved, complete ruleset under change control; successful repository and authorization sync jobs; coverage of all relevant systems and users
A large licence, a fast server, and a long history
qs.e: Deleting a risk makes conflicts disappear, so the ruleset must be governed. Stale sync means analysis of old data.

qs.x: Why does powerful access to the HANA database matter for SOX?
o: It lets someone read or change tables directly, bypassing application controls, authorizations and change documents
qs.e: Direct database access can undermine every control above it.

qs.x: Which of these is part of testing database-level privileged access?
o: Whether the default SYSTEM user is deactivated or tightly controlled
Whether the database has a logo
Whether the database name is short
Whether reports are printed in colour
qs.e: Also test who has database accounts and powerful privileges, and whether audit policies are on and reviewed independently.

None is an issue because Basis has SAP_ALL

A signed statement from the owner

qs.x: (Week 1) Section 404(a) is performed by:
qs.e: 404(a) is management’s assessment; 404(b) is the external auditor’s opinion for larger companies.

weeks.title: Testing approach, evidence, change, operations and application controls

items.name: sampling and information produced by the entity
rd: Sample size comes from the firm's or client's methodology, mainly based on how often the control runs and how risky it is. A common table is: annual 1, quarterly 2, monthly 2 to 5, weekly 5 to 15, daily 20 to 40, and many times a day 25 to 60, with higher numbers for higher risk or where we plan to rely more.
Automated controls are different: if the ITGCs are effective, I test one instance of each relevant scenario plus confirm the configuration did not change during the period.

For selection, I use random or systematic selection from a complete population and record the method and seed, so a reviewer can reproduce it. I make sure the sample covers the whole period, not just the first months.
If I find an exception, I do not quietly add more samples; I discuss with my lead whether to expand the sample or conclude the control is ineffective, following the methodology.
Completeness and accuracy of system reports

I treat it as information produced by the entity, and I need evidence that it is complete and accurate before I use it. First, how was it produced: standard SAP transaction, custom report or query, or a spreadsheet built from an extract.
Second, the parameters: I want to see them, ideally by observing the run or re-running it myself, so I know nothing was filtered out.
Third, completeness: I agree the total count or value to an independent source, such as the general ledger balance or a second report.
Fourth, accuracy: I trace a few items from the report back to the source documents in SAP and from source to report.
For a custom report, I also need comfort over the logic, either by testing it or by relying on effective change management for that program.
If the report was exported to Excel, I check that nothing was changed after export. All of this goes in the workpaper, because reviewers and external auditors look for it first.

I start with design: I inspect the tolerance configuration for invoice verification, the tolerance keys for price and quantity variances by company code, and agree them to the policy the business has approved.

Then I test operation with both a positive and a negative case. Where possible I observe, in a test system with the same configuration, an invoice within tolerance being posted and one outside tolerance being blocked for payment.
In production I can instead take existing invoices blocked for price or quantity variance and confirm the block reason matches the tolerance.
I also check who can release blocked invoices, because a strong block is pointless if anyone can release it, and I test a sample of releases for approval.

Finally, for the period, I review the configuration change logs to confirm the tolerances did not change, and I rely on effective change management ITGCs. If the tolerances changed mid-year, I test the control under both settings.

qs.x: What mainly determines sample size?
o: The methodology, based on how often the control runs and how risky it is
The size of the client’s IT department
The number of users in SAP
qs.e: A common table: annual 1, quarterly 2, monthly 2 to 5, weekly 5 to 15, daily 20 to 40, many times a day 25 to 60, with higher numbers for higher risk or planned reliance.

qs.x: How is an automated control tested if ITGCs are effective?
o: One instance of each relevant scenario, plus confirmation the configuration did not change in the period
qs.e: An automated control behaves the same way each time. If ITGCs are weak, the assumption falls away.

qs.x: Which sample selection record lets a reviewer reproduce the sample?
o: The selection method and seed, applied to a complete population
qs.e: Random or systematic selection with the method and seed recorded, covering the whole period, is reproducible.

qs.x: You find one exception in a sample of 25 for a control that must operate every time. What is the right move?
o: Agree the fact, then discuss with your lead whether to extend or conclude the control ineffective under the methodology
Quietly add more samples until the rate looks low
Delete the exception from the log
qs.e: Exceptions are evaluated, not averaged away. For a control that is expected to operate every time, one deviation in 25 is not a rounding error.

qs.x: A control owner gives you an SAP report. Which is the best first question?
o: How was it produced: standard transaction, custom report, query or a spreadsheet?
Is it printed on good paper?
qs.e: Then parameters, completeness (agree totals to an independent source), accuracy (trace items) and logic for custom reports.

items.name: change management and configuration
rd: In SAP, changes are built in development, tested in quality and imported into production through transports, managed in STMS.

To test it, I take the population of transports imported into production for the period from the import history or the transport tables, because a ticket-based population would miss unauthorized changes.
I sample transports and trace each to an approved change request, checking that approval and testing happened before the import date, and that the developer did not import their own change.

I also check that production is protected against direct changes: the client settings in SCC4 and the system change option in SE06 should not allow changes in production, and I look at the change logs for any time they were opened.
Emergency changes follow a faster path, so I test that each one was logged, reviewed and approved after the fact within the agreed time.
Finally I check who can import transports and who has developer keys in production, because that access can bypass the whole process.

I use two sources. First, the table change logs: in SAP, configuration tables can be logged, and SCU3 shows changes to logged tables with who, when, and old and new values. Before relying on it, I confirm that table logging is switched on through the system parameter for client logging, and that the specific tables I care about are flagged for logging.

Second, the transport history: configuration normally reaches production through customizing transports, so I search the import history for transports touching those tables or that configuration activity.
If both show no changes, and change management ITGCs are effective, I can conclude the setting was stable.

If logging was off, I cannot rely on the log, so I would compare the setting at the start and end of the period, test change management more heavily, and raise the missing logging with my lead as a finding in its own right.

qs.x: Where should the population of production changes come from?
o: The transport import history or transport tables for the period
qs.e: A ticket-based population would miss unauthorised changes that never had a ticket.

qs.x: Which transaction manages the transport path and shows import history?
qs.e: STMS is the transport management system. SM37 is job overview, SUIM is the user information system and SM20 is the security audit log.

qs.x: Which check shows production is protected against direct changes?
o: The client settings in SCC4 and the system change option in SE06, plus change logs for any time they were opened
The size of the transport buffer
qs.e: Production should not allow direct changes; look at the logs for any time it was open.

qs.x: Which check addresses segregation in the change process?
o: That the developer did not import their own change and that import and developer access in production is restricted
That all changes had a ticket number
qs.e: Import rights and developer keys in production can bypass the whole process.

qs.x: Table logging was off for two months of the year. What do you do?
o: Do not rely on the log: compare the setting at start and end, test change management more heavily and raise the missing logging as a finding
Rely on the log for the whole year
Treat it as no issue because nothing is visible
Switch logging on now and conclude
qs.e: Absence of evidence is only informative when the log’s coverage is established. Raise the missing logging with your lead as a finding in its own right.

items.name: operations, jobs, backups and interfaces
rd: IT operations: batch jobs and interfaces

The operations controls that matter are the ones that make sure financial transactions are processed completely and only once: scheduled batch jobs such as payment runs, depreciation, interest calculation and interfaces from other systems, plus backup and recovery.
For batch job monitoring I first identify the jobs that are financially relevant, with the process owners. Then I check who can schedule or change those jobs, because that is an access risk.

To test monitoring, I take the list of failed or cancelled jobs from SM37 for the period, sample them, and confirm each failure was noticed, investigated and resolved, for example through an incident ticket and a rerun.
For interfaces I do the same with the interface monitoring tool or error logs, and I check that reconciliations between source and SAP happen.
I also confirm that backups run and that a restore has been tested, because a backup that has never been restored is an assumption, not a control.
al: Only the approved Basis or operations team should schedule or change production financial jobs. Anyone else with that access is an access risk.
A control total checked when an interface file arrives is an interface control in transit and on receipt.

qs.x: Which transaction lists failed or cancelled batch jobs for the period?
qs.e: SM37 is the job overview used to take the list of failed jobs and sample them.

qs.x: What do you check for a sampled failed job?
o: That the failure was noticed, investigated, resolved and rerun, evidenced for example by an incident ticket
That the job name is unique
That it ran on a weekend
That the log is in English
qs.e: Monitoring means each failure is followed up to resolution.

qs.x: Who should be able to schedule production financial jobs?
o: Only the approved Basis or operations team; anyone else is an access risk
qs.e: If anyone can schedule or change a financial job, processing can be altered without a trace.

qs.x: For a third-party payroll interface into SAP, a control total checked on receipt is a control in which place?
qs.e: Record count and total amount sent with the file and checked on receipt are transit checks.

qs.x: The client says backups run every night. What would show the control is effective?
o: A test restore: a backup that has never been restored is an assumption
A statement from the Basis lead
qs.e: You need evidence the backup runs and that a restore has been tested. A failed backup should be rerun within the policy window (lab OP-03 uses 24 hours).

items.name: application controls
rd: Posting period control stops users from posting into accounting periods that are closed, which protects cut-off and means reported results cannot be changed after the close. In SAP it is configured in OB52 by posting period variant, account type and account range, and it can allow a special authorization group to keep a period open for specific users, such as the close team.

When I test it I look at four risks. Periods left open longer than the close calendar allows. Too many users in the authorization group that can post to open special periods. Broad access to maintain OB52 itself, because whoever can change it can reopen any period. And reopening without approval.

So I inspect the settings, compare them with the close calendar, review who has access to the maintenance transaction and the authorization group, and test a sample of period openings and closings, using the change logs, against approved requests.

SAP's duplicate invoice check compares new invoices against existing ones on a set of fields, typically vendor, company code, reference number, invoice date and amount. It only works if three things are true: the check is switched on for the vendors, through the vendor master flag; the system message is set to an error that blocks posting, rather than a warning users can click past; and the fields compared make sense.
Its weakness is that a small change to the reference, such as an extra dash, defeats it.
So I test design by inspecting the configuration and message settings and the vendor master flag for a sample of vendors.
Then I test effectiveness with data analysis: I extract the year's invoices and look for likely duplicates using fuzzy matching on reference, the same amount and vendor within a short window.
Any real duplicates paid show that the control, or a compensating review, is not working, and I take them to the payables team.
al: A three-way match blocks an invoice when price or quantity differ beyond tolerance from the purchase order and the goods receipt. To test it: positive and negative cases, the tolerance configuration agreed to policy, who can release blocked invoices, and the change logs for the period.

qs.x: Which is a SAP application control example?
o: The three-way match that blocks an invoice when price or quantity differ beyond tolerance
qs.e: Application controls run automatically for each transaction. The other three are manual or ITGC controls.

qs.x: How do you test a three-way match tolerance control?
o: Positive and negative cases, the tolerance configuration agreed to policy, who can release blocked invoices, and change logs for the period
qs.e: A strong block is pointless if anyone can release it. If tolerances changed mid-year, test the control under both settings.

qs.x: Which transaction configures posting periods?
qs.e: OB52 is configured by posting period variant, account type and account range.

qs.x: Which is a control risk for posting periods?
o: Too many users in the authorization group that can post to special periods, or broad access to maintain OB52
qs.e: Four risks: periods open too long, too many in the special group, broad access to maintain OB52 and reopening without approval.

qs.x: What is a known weakness of SAP’s duplicate invoice check?
o: A small change to the reference, such as an extra dash, defeats it
qs.e: Test design by inspecting configuration and the vendor flag, then test effectiveness by fuzzy matching on reference, same amount and vendor within a short window.

items.name: exceptions, workpapers and pushback
rd: A good workpaper lets an experienced reviewer who was not there understand what I did, re-perform it and reach the same conclusion without calling me.

It has a clear structure: the control and the risk it addresses, the test objective, where the population came from and how I checked it was complete, how the sample was selected, the test steps, the result for each sample with the evidence cross-referenced, any exceptions and how I evaluated them, and a conclusion that answers the objective. It is signed and dated by the preparer and the reviewer.

A reviewer sends it back when the population source is missing, when evidence does not match the sample, when exceptions are described as 'minor' without analysis, when screenshots have no date or system shown, or when the conclusion says effective but the results show a failure.
I write each workpaper as if the external auditor will read it, because they often do.
First I make sure it is really an exception: I recheck the evidence and ask the control owner for anything I might have missed, with a deadline.
If it stands, I document it straight away: what failed, which sample, the date, and what the evidence shows.

Then I work out the root cause, because that tells me whether it is a one-off, such as a reviewer on holiday with no backup, or a systemic problem, such as a control that never covered a whole entity.

Depending on the methodology, I discuss with my lead whether to extend the sample or conclude the control is not effective. I also look for compensating controls that might reduce the risk, and I consider the impact on other controls that depend on this one.

I tell my lead the same day, with the facts, my initial view on severity and the options. I never wait until the end of testing to raise an exception, and I never let the control owner fix the evidence after the fact.

Example story, to replace with your own real one: on a recent engagement, a finance manager disagreed that her monthly journal review had failed, because she said she always reviewed the journals even if she did not sign.
I prepared before the meeting: the control description, which required evidence of review, and the three months with no sign-off.

In the meeting I started by agreeing the shared goal, a clean result for her team, and then walked through the facts without blaming anyone. I asked whether there was any other evidence, such as emails with questions on specific journals.
She found one month's emails, which I accepted and documented; the other two months remained exceptions.

We agreed the root cause, the control required a sign-off she did not know about, and she proposed a simple fix: sign-off in the workflow tool. I kept my lead informed throughout, so there were no surprises.
The result was a fair finding she accepted, and a stronger control the next quarter.
If I had not had a real example, I would describe the same approach: prepare, listen, stay on the facts, accept new evidence, and escalate if we cannot agree.

qs.x: A good workpaper lets a reviewer who was not there:
o: Understand what you did, re-perform it and reach the same conclusion without calling you
qs.e: Re-performability is the standard. Write it as if the external auditor will read it.

qs.x: Which of these gets a workpaper sent back?
o: A population with no stated source
qs.e: Also: evidence that does not match the sample, exceptions called minor without analysis, undated screenshots and a conclusion that says effective when results show a failure.

qs.x: You find an exception in a sample. Which sequence is right?
o: Confirm it, document it, find root cause, assess scope and compensating controls, and escalate the same day
Wait until the end of fieldwork, then report
Ask the owner to fix the evidence
Add samples until it looks small
qs.e: Never wait until the end of fieldwork and never let the owner fix the evidence after the fact.

qs.x: A control owner disagrees with an exception. Which approach is best?
o: Prepare the facts, start from a shared goal, accept new evidence, stay on the facts and keep your lead informed
qs.e: If new evidence is produced, accept and document it. The remaining exceptions stay.

qs.x: You cannot decide whether to extend a sample. Whom do you ask?
o: Your lead, under the engagement methodology
qs.e: Do not quietly add samples. The methodology decides, with your lead.

items.note: No new reading. Re-read this week’s Monday to Friday reading boxes, and the boxes of the earlier weeks this review draws on, before you start.

o: No: it could have changed and been changed back; use the change logs for the period
Yes, the same value means no change
Yes if the ITGCs were tested last year

Rely on it because it is small
Use the GL instead without telling anyone

It is effective because it exists
