items.name: what S/4HANA changes, and reading a design document
rd: How S/4HANA changes the control landscape

Several things change. The data model is simplified: the Universal Journal brings finance and controlling postings into one table, so reports and reconciliations that relied on old tables must be rebuilt and re-tested.

Users increasingly work in Fiori apps rather than SAP GUI transactions, so access risk now involves Fiori catalogs, the OData services behind the apps and the backend roles, and the SoD ruleset must include Fiori apps and services.
Business partner replaces separate vendor and customer master transactions, so master data controls move.
Many companies also move to RISE with SAP, which shifts infrastructure and Basis controls to SAP and brings SOC 1 reliance into scope.
And the migration itself is a risk: data must be complete and accurate in the new system.
The opportunity is that S/4HANA offers more embedded analytics and automation, so some manual controls can become automated or be replaced with continuous monitoring.
I read it with the control in mind. First, the purpose: does the report give the control owner what they need to perform the control, at the right precision?
Second, the data sources: which tables and fields, and do they capture all relevant transactions, including any new S/4HANA structures.
Third, the selection screen: which parameters can users change, and could someone exclude data without it being obvious, for example a default date range or company code filter.
Fourth, the logic: calculations, groupings and exception rules, written clearly enough to test.
Fifth, security: whether the report checks authorizations, so users only see what they should.
Sixth, the test plan: I want test cases that prove completeness and accuracy, including a reconciliation to a standard report.
I feed any gaps back to the functional team before build, because fixing a design is far cheaper than failing the report as unreliable evidence at the first audit.

qs.x: Which S/4HANA change most affects reports and reconciliations that used old tables?
o: The Universal Journal brings finance and controlling postings into one table
qs.e: Reports and reconciliations that relied on old tables must be rebuilt and re-tested.

qs.x: In S/4HANA, vendor and customer master data moves to:
qs.e: Business partner replaces separate vendor and customer master transactions, so master data controls move.

qs.x: Why does Fiori change access risk testing?
o: Users work in apps backed by OData services and backend roles, so the SoD ruleset must include Fiori apps and services
Fiori removes the need for roles
qs.e: Access risk now involves catalogs, services and backend authorizations.

qs.x: A functional design document describes a new custom report used in a key control. What do you read first?
o: The purpose: does the report give the control owner what they need, at the right precision?
qs.e: Then data sources, selection parameters, logic, security and the test plan. Feed gaps back before build.

qs.x: The report’s selection screen has a default date range that users can change. Why does this matter?
o: Someone could exclude data without it being obvious, so the report may not be complete
qs.e: Selection parameters are a completeness risk for any report used as evidence.

items.name: migration and go-live
rd: Migration is where errors enter the new system for good, so I expect controls on completeness, accuracy and validity. Before migration, the data is cleansed and the mapping from old fields to new is designed and approved.
During each load, record counts and control totals are compared between the extract and what was loaded, and errors are corrected and reloaded.

After the load, the key reconciliations are done: general ledger balances by account and company code, open payables and receivables, asset values and inventory, from the old system to S/4HANA, with differences explained. Master data, such as vendor bank details, is sample-checked field by field.
Finally, the business owners sign off before go-live.

To test, I reperform a sample of the reconciliations, check that sign-offs were given before go-live, and look at access during the migration window, because migration users often have powerful access that must be removed afterwards.

I get involved from the start, because controls are cheapest to build in during design. In the prepare and explore phases, I agree the controls scope with the business and the external auditor, map current controls and identify which can become automated in S/4HANA, and write control requirements into the fit-to-standard and functional design documents.

In realize, I check that the configuration delivers those controls, that the role design is free of SoD conflicts, and I write test scripts for the automated controls so they are tested as part of integration and user acceptance testing.
In deploy, I own the cut-over controls: data migration reconciliations, approval of the migration, and access set up before go-live.
After go-live, in hypercare, I check the first period close and confirm the new controls are operating, so the first SOX cycle has evidence from day one.
Throughout, I keep the external auditor informed so they can plan reliance.

qs.x: Which control is expected during each data load?
o: Record counts and control totals compared between extract and load, with errors corrected and reloaded
qs.e: Counts and totals prove completeness during the load.

qs.x: After a migration, source and target totals match but record counts differ (5,000 against 5,012). What do you suspect?
o: Split or duplicated records whose values offset; reconcile counts and values and investigate the 12
qs.e: Matching totals with different counts suggest offsetting records. Counts and values both matter.

qs.x: Which access risk appears during the migration window?
o: Migration users often have powerful access that must be removed afterwards
qs.e: Test access during the migration window and its removal after go-live.

qs.x: When should the controls lead get involved in an S/4HANA implementation?
o: From the start, when controls are cheapest to build in during design
qs.e: Prepare and explore: agree scope and design controls. Realize: check configuration and role design. Deploy: own cut-over controls. Hypercare: check the first close.

qs.x: Business owners have not signed off the reconciliation before go-live. What do you do?
o: Raise it before go-live: sign-off is a required control, and absence is a finding
Accept it because the load worked
qs.e: Business sign-off before go-live is part of the migration control set.

items.name: Fiori, HANA and RISE
rd: Fiori access has layers. The launchpad shows tiles based on business catalogs and, in newer releases, spaces and pages assigned through roles. Showing a tile is not the real control.

To run an app, the user needs authorization to start its OData service, and then the backend authorizations decide what they can actually read or change, using the same authorization objects as the GUI transactions behind the app. So a user might not see a tile but still call the service directly if they have the authorization.
To check access, I look at the backend roles and the service authorizations, not just the catalogs.

For SoD, I make sure the GRC ruleset includes Fiori apps and their OData services and the related transaction codes, otherwise risk analysis will under-report conflicts. And I test a sample of users by checking their effective authorizations, ideally in a test system with the same roles.
RISE with SAP: who controls what

With RISE, SAP takes over the infrastructure, hosting, database and operating system administration, backups and much of the technical Basis work for the private cloud environment. Those controls move out of the client's direct testing scope and are evidenced instead by SAP's SOC 1 Type II report for the service, which customers can obtain through the SAP Trust Center.

What stays with the client is significant: user and role administration inside the SAP application, SoD and access reviews, approval and testing of changes before they are imported, the configuration of business controls, and monitoring SAP as a provider.

So in scoping I map which ITGCs are now SAP's, read the SOC 1 for those, map its complementary user entity controls to the client's controls, and keep full testing on the controls the client still owns.
A common mistake is assuming RISE covers user access. It does not.

qs.x: Is removing a Fiori tile enough to remove access?
o: No: the tile controls display only; the user may still have the backend authorizations and service access
Yes if it is done by Basis
Yes if the user logs out
qs.e: Check backend roles and service authorizations, not only catalogs.

qs.x: For SoD testing in a Fiori environment you must make sure:
o: The GRC ruleset includes Fiori apps, their OData services and related transactions
Fiori is excluded from the ruleset
qs.e: Otherwise risk analysis under-reports conflicts.

qs.x: With RISE, which controls move out of the client’s direct testing scope?
o: Infrastructure, hosting, database, operating system administration and much technical Basis work
qs.e: These are evidenced by SAP’s SOC 1 Type II. The client keeps user and role administration, SoD, access reviews, change approval and testing and business control configuration.

qs.x: A colleague says “RISE covers user access.” Best reply?
o: Incorrect: user and role administration, SoD and access reviews stay with the client
qs.e: This is the most common mistake in RISE scoping.

qs.x: On RISE, how do you test database privileged access?
o: Read SAP’s SOC 1 for those controls and focus your own testing on any database access the client keeps
qs.e: Map the report’s complementary controls to the client’s own.

items.name: SOC 1 reports
rd: SOC 1 Type I versus Type II
A SOC 1 reports on controls at a service organization that are relevant to its clients' financial reporting.
A Type I gives an opinion on whether those controls were suitably designed and implemented as of a single date.
A Type II goes further: it covers design and operating effectiveness over a period, usually six to twelve months, and lists the service auditor's tests and results control by control.

For SOX reliance over a fiscal year I need a Type II, ideally covering most of the year. A Type I only shows the controls existed on one day, so it is acceptable at most as a stop-gap, for example in a provider's first year, with extra procedures agreed with the external auditor.
I also make sure nobody accepts a SOC 2 in its place, because SOC 2 reports on security and availability criteria, not financial reporting control objectives.

Complementary user entity controls are the things the service provider says its clients must do for the provider's control objectives to be achieved. They are listed in the SOC 1 report. The service auditor's opinion assumes the client performs them, so if the client does not, the clean opinion does not protect the client.

What I do is take the list and map each one to a control in the client's risk and control matrix. Typical examples are that the client manages user access to the application, approves changes before asking the provider to import them, and reviews the provider's notifications.

Where a matching control exists, I test it as part of normal testing. Where none exists, I propose a new control with an owner and frequency and agree it with the process owner. Any CUEC that is not performed is the client's deficiency, not the provider's, and I report it that way.
A clean opinion means the service auditor concluded the control objectives were still met overall, but each exception can still matter to my client, so I assess each one.
I record what failed, the sample size and number of failures, and the provider's response.
Then I ask whether my client's environment was in the failed sample or could be affected; if the report does not say, I ask the provider in writing.
I look for compensating controls, both at the provider, such as another control in the same objective that worked, and at the client, such as a monitoring control that would catch the same problem.

Then I conclude with one of three outcomes: no impact, with the reason; impact mitigated by a named compensating control, which I then test; or impact not mitigated, which I raise as a deficiency to evaluate. Writing 'no impact' next to every exception is one of the most common findings against SOC 1 reviews.

qs.x: What does a SOC 1 Type I report cover?
o: Whether controls were suitably designed and implemented as of a single date
qs.e: Type II covers design and operating effectiveness over a period, usually six to twelve months.

qs.x: Which SOC report suits SOX reliance for the year?
o: A SOC 1 Type II covering most of the year
A SOC 1 Type I of any date
qs.e: A Type I is at most a stop-gap, for example in a provider’s first year, with extra procedures agreed with the external auditor.

qs.x: Complementary user entity controls are:
o: Controls the provider says its clients must perform for the provider’s objectives to be achieved
Controls the provider performs for itself
qs.e: The service auditor’s opinion assumes the client performs them.

qs.x: What do you do with the list of CUECs?
o: Map each to a specific client control, test it, propose a new control where none exists, and report the gaps
qs.e: A CUEC that is not performed is the client’s deficiency, not the provider’s.

qs.x: The SOC 1 opinion is clean but Section IV lists three exceptions. What do you do?
o: Assess each one: what failed, whether your client could be affected, compensating controls, then conclude no impact, mitigated or deficiency
Accept the clean opinion and write no impact
Ask the provider to remove them
qs.e: Writing no impact next to every exception is one of the most common failures.

items.name: bridge letters, carve-out and SOC 2
rd: That is a six-month gap, which is long. I would first request a bridge letter from the provider covering 1 July to 31 December.

A bridge letter is a statement from the provider's management that the controls have not changed materially and that they know of no failures since the report period. It is not audited, so on its own it is weak for a gap this long.

I would therefore discuss with the external auditor what else is needed, and lean on the client's own controls over the provider for those six months: for example the monthly reconciliation of the provider's output to the ledger, reviews of service reports and incidents, and the client's review of changes. I would test those controls for the gap period.
I would also check when the provider's next report is due, in case it arrives in time, and read the bridge letter carefully for mentions of changes, such as a new data centre.
Service organizations often rely on other providers, called subservice organizations, such as a co-location data centre.
Under the inclusive method, the subservice organization's relevant controls are included in the description and tested within the same SOC 1 report.

Under the carve-out method, they are excluded: the report describes what the subservice organization does and lists the controls the provider expects it to have, called complementary subservice organization controls, but does not test them.
It matters because, under carve-out, part of the control chain my client relies on has not been examined in that report.

So I identify every carved-out provider, decide whether its controls matter to my client's financial reporting, and if they do, obtain evidence about them, usually the subservice organization's own SOC 1, or check that the provider monitors it effectively. I record this in the reliance memo.
al: A SOC 2 reports on security, availability and related criteria, not on financial reporting control objectives. It does not replace a SOC 1 for SOX reliance.

qs.x: The provider’s SOC 1 ends 30 June and the client’s year ends 31 December. What do you request first?
o: A bridge letter for 1 July to 31 December, and discuss further evidence with the external auditor
qs.e: A bridge letter is unaudited management assurance. For a six-month gap lean also on the client’s own controls over the provider.

qs.x: What is the main limitation of a bridge letter?
o: It is a management statement and is not audited, so alone it is weak for a long gap
qs.e: Read it for mentions of changes, such as a new data centre.

qs.x: Under the carve-out method, a subservice organisation’s controls are:
o: Excluded from testing in the report
qs.e: The report lists complementary subservice organisation controls but does not test them.

qs.x: A provider uses a carved-out data centre. What do you do?
o: Decide whether its controls matter to your client’s financial reporting and obtain evidence, usually its own SOC 1
Test it with the provider’s own people
qs.e: Record the decision in the workpaper.

qs.x: A client offers a SOC 2 in place of a SOC 1. Do you accept it?
o: No: a SOC 2 reports on security and availability criteria, not financial reporting control objectives
Yes if it is Type II
qs.e: SOC 2 does not substitute for SOC 1 in SOX reliance.

items.name: Week 4 review (with spaced questions)
items.note: No new reading. Re-read this week’s Monday to Friday reading boxes, and the boxes of the earlier weeks this review draws on, before you start.

qs.x: An exception in the SOC 1 relates to a control your client relies on, and no compensating control exists. Which outcome?
o: Impact not mitigated: raise it as a deficiency to evaluate
qs.e: The three outcomes are no impact with reason, mitigated by a named tested control, or not mitigated and raised.

qs.x: A CUEC says the client must review provider notifications. There is no such control. What do you propose?
o: A new control with an owner and frequency, agreed with the process owner
qs.e: Any CUEC not performed is the client’s deficiency.

qs.x: You scope a RISE client. Which controls do you fully test yourself?
o: Those the client still owns: user administration, SoD, change approval and business configuration
All of them in the same way
qs.e: Map which ITGCs are now SAP’s and read the SOC 1 for those.

qs.x: (Week 3) A tolerance configuration is asserted unchanged. What two sources do you use?
o: Table change logs and the transport history
The user list and the backup log
The HR file and a ticket
qs.e: If both show no change and change management is effective, the setting was stable.

qs.x: (Week 3) Which job-related access test matters most?
o: Who can schedule or change financially relevant jobs
qs.e: Scheduling access is an access risk.

qs.x: (Week 2) Why is permanent SAP_ALL in production serious?
o: It undermines both access and change controls and may affect reliance on other controls
qs.e: Raise it with your lead the same day.

weeks.title: AI, automation, stakeholders and behavioural answers

items.name: using AI in SOX work, and its limits
rd: Where AI helps in control testing

I use AI where there is volume and pattern work. For example, triaging hundreds of SoD conflicts into mitigated, unused and active groups using the GRC export and usage data; matching transports imported to production against change tickets; and drafting test steps or workpaper wording from my notes. It saves hours and lets me spend time on judgement.

Where I do not trust it is anything that needs to be proven or judged. An AI statement is never evidence; the system report is. It can invent an answer if the data it needs is missing, so I tell it to use only the data I give it and to list anything it cannot decide.
And severity of a deficiency is a professional judgement that stays with me and my lead.
I always verify a sample of its output in SAP, save the prompt and output with the workpaper, and only use tools the firm and client have approved, with personal data masked.

Continuous controls monitoring means using automated rules to check transactions, configuration or access frequently, often daily, instead of relying on periodic manual reviews or year-end sampling. Exceptions are sent to an owner who must investigate and close them.

In SAP it can be done with SAP Process Control, with GRC Access Control alerts, or with analytics tools on extracted data. Examples include flagging changes to vendor bank details followed by a payment within a few days, monitoring for new SoD conflicts or firefighter use, detecting duplicate invoices, and alerting on changes to key configuration such as tolerances or posting periods.

For it to work as a control, the rules must be designed and tested, the data feeding them must be complete, and every exception must be worked and evidenced. Otherwise it becomes a report nobody reads.
Done well, it lets a company replace some manual controls and find problems in days rather than at year end.
I would want six things documented on every AI-assisted workpaper. The tool used and confirmation it is approved for client data.
The inputs: the original system export with its parameters and a completeness check, because the AI's output is only as good as its input.
The exact prompt and the unedited output, saved with the date.
The verification: which items the preparer checked in the system and what they found, including any errors the AI made.
A conclusion written and signed by the preparer and reviewed by me, never phrased as 'per AI'.
And how personal data was handled.

I would agree with the external auditor at planning where we intend to use AI and how we will document it, so there are no surprises at year end. When I review, I check those six items first, before I look at the conclusion.
Controls over a GenAI controls tool
I would treat the tool as an in-scope system, because its output will support SOX conclusions.
The main risks are wrong or invented results, incomplete inputs, unnoticed changes to prompts or models, and people over-relying on it.

So I would ask for: requirements traced to the risk and control matrix, so it is clear which control steps it performs; input controls proving the data it receives is complete and accurate; a test set with known answers, re-run whenever the prompt, model or configuration changes; change management over prompts and model versions, just like code; access controls over who can change it; logging of every run, including inputs and outputs; and mandatory human review and sign-off of its conclusions.

I would also involve the external auditor early, because if they cannot rely on the tool, the savings disappear. A lead's job here is to translate the control matrix into clear functional requirements the developers can build and test against.
al: An AI summary is a pointer, not evidence. Read Section IV (the exceptions) of a SOC 1 yourself.

qs.x: Which use of AI in SOX testing is generally acceptable?
o: Drafting test steps or summarising a policy, with the output checked by a person who understands the control
Letting AI conclude a control is effective
Pasting the client’s full ledger into a public chatbot
qs.e: AI assists; a named person remains accountable for every conclusion.

qs.x: The six items to document when an AI tool contributes to a workpaper include:
o: What it was used for, the tool and version, the input given, the output received, who checked it and how, and what was changed
qs.e: Together they let a reviewer re-perform and trust the step.

qs.x: An AI tool summarises 40 pages of SOC 1 text and says “no exceptions”. What do you do?
o: Read Section IV yourself; the summary is a pointer, not evidence
qs.e: Exceptions are exactly what a summary can drop.

qs.x: What does continuous controls monitoring (CCM) change?
o: It tests whole populations automatically and often, instead of samples once a period
It removes the need for control owners
It removes the need for ITGCs
qs.e: CCM still depends on trusted data, a stable rule set and independent review of alerts.

qs.x: A CCM rule stopped running in March and no one noticed. What is the control issue?
o: The monitoring of the monitoring: failure of the tool must itself be detected and followed up
qs.e: A silent failure is a design gap, and months of coverage are lost.

items.name: AI data safety and AI-drafted procedures
rd: Using AI on client data safely

That is a confidentiality and data protection problem. The client's data, including personal data, has gone to a service the firm and client have not approved, and we cannot be sure how it is stored or used.

I would ask my colleague to stop and not paste anything more, and I would raise it with our lead straight away, without blaming, because the firm will have an incident process and may need to inform the client or its data protection officer. I would not try to quietly fix it myself.

Then I would help redo the analysis the right way: using the AI tool the firm has approved for client work, masking names with codes and keeping the key separately, and saving the prompt and output with the workpaper.
Afterwards, I would suggest a short reminder to the team on the AI rules, because these mistakes usually come from people trying to save time, not from bad intent.
I would check it against a short list. Is there a step to prove the user list given to reviewers was complete, by comparing it with a system extract at the same date? AI drafts often miss this.
Does the sample size follow our methodology for a quarterly control, usually two quarters, rather than an inflated number?
Are the SAP sources right, for example user and role data from SUIM or the GRC reports, and do they exist in this system?
Does it test that requested removals were actually processed, by tracing them to change documents?
Is the reviewer independent of the security team?
And could another tester re-perform the steps from what is written?
I would correct the draft, mark it as reviewed by me, and keep the original output and my changes with the workpaper.
al: A drafted step that names a table or transaction that does not exist shows the draft was not grounded in the system. Verify every technical reference.

qs.x: Which data may NOT go into a public AI tool?
o: Client confidential data and personal data
A generic definition of a term
qs.e: Use only approved tools and agreements; ask what the engagement terms allow.

qs.x: You want AI help with a screenshot containing user names. What do you do?
o: Remove or mask the personal data first, or use an approved internal tool
qs.e: Minimise data: share only what the task needs.

qs.x: An AI drafts a procedure for a sampling test. What do you check before use?
o: Each step against the methodology and the actual system, and that population, sample and evidence are all stated
qs.e: AI drafts often miss completeness and accuracy checks on the population.

qs.x: The AI-drafted step names a transaction code that does not exist in the client’s release. What does that tell you?
o: The draft was not grounded in the system; verify every technical reference
It is a typo to ignore
qs.e: Hallucinated references are a known AI risk, so verify them.

qs.x: Your colleague says it is fine to use a free personal AI account for client work to save time. Best response?
o: Explain the confidentiality risk and use the approved tool
Report the colleague first without talking
qs.e: Speak up early and kindly, and follow the engagement terms.

items.name: behavioural and honest answers
rd: A strong answer follows past, present and future in about two minutes.

Example, to adapt with your own details: 'I started my career in finance operations, where I worked with SAP every day and saw how a small control failure, such as a missed vendor bank check, could turn into a real loss. That got me interested in controls.

Over the past year I have trained in SAP controls testing: I have tested ITGCs and segregation of duties on a live SAP lab system, worked through 90 audit procedures with evidence packs, and practised SOC 1 reviews and AI-assisted testing. What I enjoy most is finding the root cause of a control gap and helping the business fix it in a practical way.

I am applying for this role because your team works on SAP S/4HANA and GRC, which is exactly where I want to build my career, and I would bring both a business view and hands-on testing skills from day one.'
Moving into controls without a Big 4 background
I would answer the gap directly and then show evidence. 'You are right that I have not worked at a Big 4 firm.

What I have done is learn and practise the same work: I have tested ITGCs and segregation of duties on a live SAP lab system, worked through 90 SAP audit procedures with worked examples and evidence packs, written a SOC 1 reliance memo, and practised the deficiency evaluation and remediation steps your team carries out.

I bring something extra as well: I have worked inside the business with SAP, so I understand how control owners think and what makes a control practical rather than theoretical. That helps me get evidence on time and recommend fixes that actually get implemented.
Show adaptability and invite a test
I know every firm has its own methodology, and I am used to learning structured methods quickly. I would welcome a test of my skills, for example a short case on a user access review.'

Use the situation, task, action, result structure with your own example. Model: 'Two weeks before a quarter-end testing deadline, I had twelve controls left and two of my evidence providers were on leave.
I listed the controls and ranked them by risk and by how close they were to done; the key access and change controls came first because other controls depended on them.

I told my lead the same day which three controls were at risk and proposed a plan: I would finish the high-risk ones first, ask the providers' backups for evidence, and move two low-risk controls to the following week with the auditor's agreement. I blocked time for focused testing and kept a short daily update.
We concluded ten controls on time, including all the high-risk ones, and the other two a week later with no surprises for the auditor.
What I learned is to raise risk early, because it gives everyone options.'
al: When you lack an experience, state what you have done, what you have studied and built (labs, project) and how you would close the gap. Never claim what you cannot defend with the next question.

qs.x: What is the best structure for a behavioural answer?
o: Situation, your actions, result and what you learned, in about two minutes
A long background and no result
qs.e: Use I, not we, for your own actions.

qs.x: You are asked about a mistake you made. Which is strongest?
o: A real, modest mistake, what you did to fix it and what you changed afterwards
A mistake that was not yours
qs.e: Honesty plus ownership plus change builds trust.

qs.x: You do not know the answer to a technical question. What do you do?
o: Say what you know, say what you would check and how, and do not guess
qs.e: Panels reward honest reasoning more than bluffing.

qs.x: You are asked about S/4HANA experience you do not have. Best answer?
o: State what you have done, what you have studied and built (labs, project) and how you would close the gap
qs.e: Never claim what you cannot defend with the next question.

qs.x: Which sentence is a good teach-back of a control to a panel?
o: “The control is X, the risk is Y, I test it by Z, and if it fails I would do W.”
qs.e: Teach-back in plain words proves understanding.

items.name: executive communication and auditor disagreement
rd: Explaining a finding to a senior executive

I would lead with the business impact, not the technical detail, and keep it to four points. What happened: 'Five people in IT could change vendor bank details and approve payments without anyone checking.'
Why it matters: 'That means a fraudulent payment could have been made without being caught; we found no evidence it happened, but we cannot rely on the control this year.'
What is being done: 'Access has been removed, a daily review of bank changes starts next week, and we are checking every bank change made this year.'
What I need: 'Your support for the finance team to complete that review by month end, and awareness that this may be reported to the audit committee as a significant deficiency.'
I would have the detail ready if asked, but I would not start with transaction codes or authorization objects. Executives remember the risk, the action and the ask.

I start by understanding exactly what concerns them: is it the design, the evidence, the sample, or how I evaluated an exception? I ask them to point to the specific gap, and I take it seriously, because they may have seen something I missed.
Then I go back to the workpaper and evidence. If they are right, I say so, correct the conclusion and fix the root cause in our approach.

If I still believe the control is effective, I set out the facts calmly: the control design, the evidence for each sample and how it meets the methodology, and anything that addresses their concern. Often more evidence or a short extra test resolves it.
I bring my lead in early rather than at the end, and if we still disagree, the lead and the auditor's manager resolve it. I document the discussion and the outcome in the workpaper.
The relationship matters for the whole engagement, so I keep the tone collaborative: we both want a reliable conclusion.
al: Disagreement with the external auditor: ask for their reasoning, compare facts and criteria, bring your lead in, and do not argue or concede on the spot.
If new facts change the picture, update the conclusion and say so openly.
If management asks you to soften a finding, the facts and the classification under the criteria stay fixed. Wording can improve clarity but not change meaning.

qs.x: How do you explain a deficiency to a non-technical executive?
o: Lead with the business risk and what it means, then the fact and the fix and the date
qs.e: Executives want risk, effect, owner and timing.

qs.x: Which opening is best for an executive update?
o: “We found one issue that could let a payment be made without approval. It is fixed by 15 December.”
qs.e: Plain, short, specific.

qs.x: The external auditor disagrees with your classification of a deficiency. First move?
o: Ask for their reasoning, compare facts and criteria, and bring your lead in; do not argue or concede on the spot
qs.e: Seek understanding of the basis, then decide with your lead.

qs.x: New facts you had not seen change the picture. What do you do?
o: Update the conclusion and say so openly
qs.e: Changing a conclusion on new facts is professional, not weak.

qs.x: Management asks you to soften the wording of a finding. What stays fixed?
o: The facts and the classification under the criteria; wording can improve clarity but not change meaning
qs.e: You can improve tone but not the substance.

items.name: deadlines, panel questions and GenAI controls
rd: Always have three or four questions ready, tailored to the interviewer. Strong examples: 'What would success look like in this role after the first 90 days?'
'Which SAP systems and GRC tools does the team work with today, and are there changes coming, such as a move to S/4HANA or RISE?'
'What are the biggest control challenges the team is facing this year?'
'How does the team work with the external auditor, and how much do they rely on your testing?'
'How is the team using AI or automation in testing, and where do you want to go next?'
For a supervisor: 'How do you like updates and questions from your team?'
Save questions about salary and benefits for the recruiter or a later stage. End by thanking them and briefly restating why you are a good fit.
al: Deadline at risk: tell your lead early, with what is done, what is left, the new date and the options.
No time left: protect the most risky tests and the quality of evidence, and agree scope reductions in writing with your lead.
GenAI controls: an approved-use policy, access control, review of outputs, and logging of prompts and results.
How would you use AI here? Name specific uses, the checks and the limits, including data safety and human accountability.
Sharp challenge from a panel: stay calm, restate in your own words, accept a fair point, and hold your ground with facts where you are right.

qs.x: You will miss a deadline. What do you do?
o: Tell your lead early with what is done, what is left, the new date and the options
Work quietly all night and say nothing
qs.e: Early, specific warning with options.

qs.x: You are asked to test a control with no time left. What do you protect?
o: The most risky tests and the quality of evidence; agree scope reductions in writing with your lead
qs.e: Prioritise by risk and make the trade-off visible.

qs.x: Which GenAI control matters for a client using AI in financial reporting?
o: An approved-use policy, access control, review of outputs and logging of prompts and results
qs.e: Treat the AI tool like any other system touching financial data: access, change, output review and logging.

qs.x: A panel member asks: how would you use AI on this project? Best answer?
o: Name specific uses, the checks and the limits, including data safety and human accountability
qs.e: Balance value with control.

qs.x: A panel member challenges your answer sharply. Best response?
o: Stay calm, restate in your words, accept a fair point and hold your ground with facts where you are right
qs.e: Composure and facts matter more than winning.

items.name: Week 5 review (with spaced questions)
items.note: No new reading. Re-read this week’s Monday to Friday reading boxes, and the boxes of the earlier weeks this review draws on, before you start.

qs.x: An AI-assisted workpaper has a conclusion but no record of the checks. What is missing?
o: Who checked it and how, so a reviewer cannot rely on it
qs.e: Documentation of the AI use and review is part of the evidence.

qs.x: Which wording best states a finding to an executive?
o: Risk first, then fact, owner and date
qs.e: Executives act on risk, owner and date.

qs.x: (Week 4) You list CUECs and one is not performed. Where does the deficiency sit?
o: With the client, not the provider
qs.e: The provider’s opinion assumes the client performs the CUEC.

qs.x: (Week 2) An access review passed sign-off. Which extra check shows it worked?
o: That requested removals appear in SAP change documents
That the form was signed twice
qs.e: Closed sign-off does not equal removal.

qs.x: (Week 3) A daily control has 40 operating instances in the year. Which sample size is typical?
qs.e: Daily controls typically have 20 to 40 items.

qs.x: (Week 3) A backup is said to run nightly. What is the decisive evidence?
o: A tested restore as well as the job log
qs.e: Never-restored backups are assumptions.

items.name: scoping and the first two weeks
rd: Your first two weeks as controls lead

In week one I take control and find the fires. I meet my sponsor and the external auditor to understand what they expect and what worries them. I read the scope, the risk and control matrix and the testing tracker, and I check them against reality with the team, because trackers on late engagements are usually optimistic.

I start a RAID log of risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, and I pick the two or three issues that could stop the engagement, typically missing evidence, unavailable control owners or unclear scope, and act on them.

In week two I re-baseline the plan with realistic dates and owners, agree it with the sponsor, and set a weekly rhythm: a team stand-up, a status report with clear measures, and a meeting with the external auditor.
I also aim for an early win, such as closing a backlog of evidence requests, to rebuild confidence.
What I avoid is changing the methodology or the team in the first days before I understand why we are behind.
Scoping a new SAP controls engagement
I ask questions in four areas. Business and audit: which entities and accounts are significant, what the external auditor plans to rely on, and what deficiencies were found last year.
Systems: the SAP landscape, which systems and clients feed financial reporting, the database and operating system, interfaces, and any planned changes such as an S/4HANA move.
Third parties: hosting, RISE, payroll or other providers, and whether SOC 1 reports exist.
And people: who owns each process and IT area, and who will provide evidence.
I request the system landscape diagram, the previous year's control matrix and findings, user and role listings, and the change and incident processes.

From that I produce a scoping memo explaining what is in and out of scope and why, an updated risk and control matrix, a test plan with timing and sample sizes, a resource plan, and an evidence request list. I agree all of it with the client and the external auditor before testing starts.
al: Briefing a junior on day one: what the project is, their tasks, how the workpaper standard works, how to escalate and when to ask.

qs.x: Which question helps set scope at the start of a SOX project?
o: Which systems, entities and processes are in scope, and who decides?
qs.e: Scoping questions include systems, entities, key reports, third parties, prior-year deficiencies and the timeline.

qs.x: What do you do in the first two weeks as the senior owner?
o: Confirm scope and timeline, meet owners, agree the RCM, set up the evidence tracker and weekly status, and brief the junior
qs.e: Set the foundation before testing: scope, plan, tools, rules and roles.

qs.x: The client wants to begin testing before scope is agreed. What do you do?
o: Explain the rework risk and agree a minimal scope in writing first
qs.e: Unwritten scope becomes a dispute later.

qs.x: Prior-year deficiencies exist. How do they shape this year’s plan?
o: They get follow-up testing first and affect risk ratings and sample sizes
They are only for the report
qs.e: Remediation must be re-tested.

qs.x: How do you brief a junior on day one?
o: What the project is, their tasks, how the workpaper standard works, how to escalate and when to ask
Hand over a list and leave
qs.e: A clear brief, with standards and an escalation route, prevents rework.

items.name: the risk and control matrix
rd: Building and owning the control matrix

I build it top-down: from significant accounts and assertions to the risks of material misstatement in each process, then the key controls that address each risk, and finally the IT general controls over the systems those controls depend on.

Each control row needs clear attributes: a unique ID, a description precise enough to test, the risk it addresses, owner, frequency, type (preventive or detective), nature (manual, automated or IT-dependent manual), the system and any key reports used, and the evidence expected.
I walk it through with each control owner, so they recognise their control as written, and agree it with the external auditor before testing.

During the year I keep it right with change control: any change to a process, system, role or owner comes to me, is assessed for impact on the matrix, updated with a version history, and communicated to testers and the auditor. A matrix that nobody updates after March is one of the most common causes of year-end surprises.
al: A key risk with no control: record a design gap, raise it, and consider whether a compensating control exists.
Two controls on the same risk: test the key one and treat the other as secondary unless the methodology says otherwise, and document why.
If the design changed mid-year, test the control under both versions for the periods each applied.

qs.x: What is the risk and control matrix (RCM) for?
o: It links each risk to the control that addresses it, with owner, frequency, type and test plan
qs.e: The RCM drives scoping, testing and reporting.

qs.x: A key risk has no control in the RCM. What do you do?
o: Record a design gap, raise it, and consider whether a compensating control exists
qs.e: A missing control is a finding in itself.

qs.x: Two controls address the same risk. Do you test both?
o: Test the key one and treat the other as secondary unless the methodology says otherwise, documenting why
qs.e: Select key controls by risk and reliance and document the choice.

qs.x: Which attributes belong in each RCM row?
o: Control ID, description, owner, frequency, type (manual or automated), system, key flag, test procedure and evidence
qs.e: Without them the test cannot be planned.

qs.x: The RCM was updated mid-year after a process change. What do you test?
o: The control under both versions for the periods they applied
qs.e: Change in design splits the testing period.

items.name: classification and remediation
rd: A deficiency exists when a control's design or operation does not allow staff to prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis.
To decide severity I look at two questions: how likely is it that the failure could lead to a misstatement, and how big could that misstatement be.
A material weakness is a deficiency, or combination, where there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on time.
A significant deficiency is less severe than that but important enough to merit the attention of those overseeing financial reporting, such as the audit committee.

In practice I document the facts, the accounts and amounts exposed, any compensating controls that operated and at what precision, and whether several deficiencies in the same area combine to something worse. An ITGC failure is assessed by its effect on the application controls and reports that depend on it.
I bring a proposed rating with reasoning to my lead; final classification is agreed with management and the external auditor.

I work back from year end. A remediated control usually has to operate for a minimum period before it can be retested, for example one or two cycles for a monthly control, so I calculate the latest date each fix must be in place.
Then I prioritise by severity: anything that could be a significant deficiency or material weakness first.
For each deficiency I agree with the owner a clear root cause, the fix, what 'done' looks like, a date, and the evidence that will prove it.

I track them on one remediation tracker and review it weekly with the owners and monthly with the sponsor. Where an owner misses a date, I escalate quickly and early, using the escalation ladder: first a direct conversation, then their manager, then the sponsor.

I also plan retesting with the external auditor so they know when to expect results. Where a fix cannot be in place in time, I tell the sponsor early so the impact on the year-end assessment can be managed honestly.

qs.x: A material weakness is:
o: A deficiency, or combination, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis
qs.e: A significant deficiency is less severe but merits attention by those overseeing financial reporting.

qs.x: Which factors do you weigh in classifying a deficiency?
o: The likelihood and magnitude of misstatement, the accounts affected, compensating controls and whether it was detected or exploited
qs.e: Classification is judgement under the criteria; your lead and the auditor are involved.

qs.x: When should remediation be done to count for the year?
o: Early enough that the fixed control operates for long enough to be tested before year end
Any time before the report is signed
qs.e: A fix without operating time cannot be shown effective.

qs.x: The client fixes a control the week before year end. What do you tell them?
o: It may be too late to show it operating for the year; agree what evidence and sample is possible and report honestly
qs.e: The original deficiency still stands for the period before the fix.

qs.x: A single exception in a key control that has strong compensating controls. Classification?
o: Evaluate: it may be a control deficiency, mitigated by the compensating control, documented and agreed with your lead
qs.e: The compensating control must be tested too.

items.name: status, KPIs and reviewing a junior
rd: I keep it to one page, every week, in the same format. At the top, an overall status in red, amber or green with one sentence on why.
Then a few measures. Testing progress: controls tested and concluded against the plan, by area.
Evidence: requests outstanding and how many are overdue by owner, because overdue evidence is the best early warning of a late finish.
Exceptions and deficiencies: how many are open, their likely severity and remediation status, with anything that could be a significant deficiency or material weakness called out by name.
Then the top risks and issues from the RAID log with owners and dates, and finally the decisions or help I need from the sponsor.

I base every number on the tracker so it can be checked. The rule I follow is no surprises: if something is going wrong, the sponsor hears it from me first, with a plan, not at the end of the quarter.
I review in a set order so I catch what matters first. Is the population complete and is its source documented?
Does the sample follow the methodology?
Does the evidence for each sample actually show the control operated, and is it dated and from the right system?
Are exceptions properly evaluated? And does the conclusion match the results?
Formatting comes last. I record review points in the workpaper or tracker, so they are cleared and visible to the auditor, rather than fixing things myself.

For feedback, I sit with the tester for the first few workpapers, explain why each point matters, for example why an undated screenshot is not evidence, and ask them to fix it themselves. I look for patterns rather than single errors, and I give praise for good work in the same detail. Over a few weeks the review points should fall, and I use that as my measure of whether the coaching is working.

qs.x: Which content belongs in a weekly status report?
o: Progress against plan, exceptions found, risks and issues, open requests and next steps
qs.e: Status should let a manager decide without a call.

qs.x: Which KPIs show testing health?
o: Tests completed against plan, exceptions open and closed, evidence requests overdue and review turnaround
qs.e: Choose measures that drive decisions.

qs.x: In what order do you review a junior’s workpaper?
o: Scope and population first, then sample, evidence match, result, exceptions and conclusion
qs.e: Fix foundations first; errors early cascade.

qs.x: The junior’s workpaper has a wrong population. What do you do?
o: Send it back with a clear explanation and an example, and check the other tests built on the same source
qs.e: Coach, and check for the same error elsewhere.

qs.x: Your status shows a delay caused by late evidence. How do you word it?
o: State the cause, the effect on the date and the action you need from the client
qs.e: Be factual and ask for a specific action.

items.name: the whole Thornfield spine and rookie mistakes
al: Project order: onboarding and mobilisation, planning and scoping, understanding the RCM, test planning, evidence extraction, interim testing (access, then change and operations), SOC 1 reliance, exceptions and findings, remediation and retesting, roll-forward, review and close-out.

Rookie mistakes: sampling from a population the control owner supplied without checking completeness; waiting to report exceptions; writing “no impact” against every SOC 1 exception; treating sign-off as proof of removal.
A conclusion of “effective” cannot stand over an unexplained exception: evaluate the exception first.
Three questions for any evidence: is it complete, is it accurate, and does it cover the whole period?
A senior owns scope, judgement, review and communication, not just the performing of tests.

qs.x: Which order do the project phases follow?
o: Onboarding, planning and scoping, understanding the RCM, test planning, evidence extraction, interim testing, SOC 1 reliance, findings, remediation, roll-forward, review and close-out
qs.e: The spine runs from onboarding to review and close-out, with remediation and roll-forward after the findings.

qs.x: Which is a common rookie mistake?
o: Sampling from a population provided by the control owner without checking completeness
qs.e: Others: waiting to report exceptions, accepting “no impact” on SOC exceptions, and mistaking sign-off for removal.

qs.x: A workpaper concludes “effective” but has one unexplained exception. Verdict?
o: Wrong: an unexplained exception must be evaluated before concluding
Right if the sample was large
qs.e: Conclusions must match results.

qs.x: Which three questions apply to any piece of evidence?
o: Is it complete, is it accurate and does it cover the whole period?
Is it pretty, is it long and is it signed?
Is it cheap, is it fast and is it new?
Is it in English, in PDF and in colour?
qs.e: Completeness, accuracy and coverage of the period.

qs.x: Overall, what makes a senior consultant different from a junior?
o: Owning scope, judgement, review and communication, not just performing tests
qs.e: Seniors own the whole project and the junior’s output.

items.name: Week 6 review (with spaced questions)
items.note: No new reading. Re-read this week’s Monday to Friday reading boxes, and the boxes of the earlier weeks this review draws on, before you start.

qs.x: A control failed all year and compensating controls are untested. Likely classification direction?
o: Potentially a significant deficiency or material weakness, pending evaluation of compensating controls
qs.e: Untested compensating controls cannot mitigate.

qs.x: What does your weekly status say about an open exception?
o: Facts, root cause so far, scope, owner and next date
qs.e: Keep it factual and forward-looking.

qs.x: What is the first thing the junior should receive?
o: A brief with scope, standards and escalation route
qs.e: A clear brief prevents rework.

qs.x: (Week 2) A leaver locked late with activity after the leave date. Severity?
o: Higher: late removal with activity needs investigation
qs.e: Activity after the leave date raises the risk.

qs.x: (Week 4) Which report supports reliance for the whole year?
qs.e: Type II covers operating effectiveness over a period.

qs.x: (Week 5) Who is accountable for an AI-assisted conclusion?
o: A named person on the team
qs.e: A person remains accountable.

final.name: Final exam
final.note: Thirty questions, no notes. Pass: 24 or more. Distinction: 27 or more.

qs.x: What is your first step on the 131 against 120 difference?
o: Identify and explain the 11 unmatched users before sampling
Ask the owner to delete them
qs.e: The gap may hide unauthorised access, so explain it first.
qs.ss: Thornfield Components runs SAP ECC with a custom GRC ruleset. Your population of users created in the year, taken from USR02, has 131 users. The ticket tool shows 120 access requests. A SUIM report shows three named finance users with SAP_ALL in production. The quarterly access review was signed off on time, but a sample of ten requested removals shows only six reflected in SAP change documents.

qs.x: What do you do about the three finance users with SAP_ALL?
o: Establish reason and approval, review their activity from logs and change documents, and raise it with your lead the same day
Remove the profile without telling anyone
Report it only at year end
qs.e: Facts, activity, escalation.

qs.x: What is your conclusion on the access review?
o: Sign-off exists but the review did not operate effectively for removals; evaluate as an exception and extend per methodology
qs.e: Four of ten removals did not happen.

qs.x: The business claims a monthly manager review mitigates the SoD conflicts. What do you do?
o: Test whether the review addresses the specific risk, is independent, precise and evidenced for the whole period
qs.e: Mitigation must fit the risk and operate.

qs.x: Why use the transport history as your population?
o: It captures imports that had no ticket
qs.e: Ticket-based populations miss unauthorised changes.
qs.ss: For the year, the transport import history shows 214 production imports; the change tickets total 205. SCC4 shows production set to “no changes allowed”, but the change log shows it was open for two days in August. Table logging for a key pricing table was switched off between April and May. A nightly payment-file job failed on 9 dates; evidence of follow-up exists for six.

qs.x: What do you do about the nine imports with no ticket?
o: Trace each to who imported it and why; treat unexplained ones as exceptions and raise them
qs.e: Unexplained imports are potential unauthorised changes.

qs.x: How does the logging gap affect your work?
o: You cannot rely on the log for those two months; add procedures and raise the gap as a finding
Switch it on and move on
qs.e: Absence of logs is a limitation and a finding.

qs.x: What do you conclude on the three failed jobs without follow-up?
o: Exceptions to the monitoring control; investigate the impact on payments and evaluate
qs.e: Each failure needs resolution evidence.

qs.x: Which control area needs re-design first because of the business partner change?
o: Vendor master change and approval controls and related SoD rules
qs.e: Master data controls move to the new object.
qs.ss: Thornfield is moving to S/4HANA on RISE. Vendor master data moves to the business partner, Fiori apps replace several GUI transactions, and the data migration has matching totals but 5,000 versus 5,012 records. The provider’s SOC 1 Type II runs 1 January to 30 June; the year end is 31 December. The CUEC list includes “review provider notifications” and the report has two exceptions in Section IV.

qs.x: What do you do about the 5,000 versus 5,012?
o: Reconcile counts and values and investigate the extra 12 before sign-off
qs.e: Counts and values both matter.

qs.x: What do you request for 1 July to 31 December?
o: A bridge letter and additional evidence, agreed with the external auditor
qs.e: A bridge letter is unaudited assurance.

qs.x: How do you treat the two Section IV exceptions?
o: Assess each for impact on the client and conclude no impact, mitigated or deficiency with reasons
qs.e: Each needs reasoned analysis.

qs.x: What does the non-existent table tell you?
o: The draft was not grounded in the system; verify all technical references
qs.e: Hallucinated references are a known AI risk.
qs.ss: A junior used an AI tool to draft a test procedure and summarise a 60-page SOC 1. The procedure cites a table that does not exist in the client release. The summary says “no exceptions”. The junior pasted a screenshot containing user names into a public chatbot. The workpaper population came from a spreadsheet supplied by the control owner.

qs.x: How do you handle the SOC 1 summary?
o: Read Section IV yourself and treat the summary as a pointer
qs.e: Summaries can drop exceptions.

qs.x: What do you do about the screenshot?
o: Report it to your lead, assess the exposure under the engagement terms and set the rule with the junior
qs.e: Raise it early and fix the practice.

qs.x: What do you do about the spreadsheet population?
o: Prove it complete and accurate against an independent source before sampling
qs.e: Information produced by the entity must be validated.

qs.x: What is your first move on the 3 of 25?
o: Confirm the facts and root cause, assess scope and discuss extending or concluding under the methodology with your lead
qs.e: Never quietly add samples.
qs.ss: It is week 5. A key control failed in 3 of 25 samples. Compensating controls are not yet tested. The client fixed the control last week and wants it called effective. The external auditor believes the deficiency is a material weakness; you think it is a significant deficiency. Your junior’s workpaper concludes “effective” with an unexplained exception.

qs.x: How do you treat the fix made last week?
o: It does not erase the failure for the period; test what operating evidence exists and report honestly
qs.e: The deficiency stands for the earlier period.

qs.x: How do you handle the disagreement with the external auditor?
o: Understand their reasoning, compare facts and criteria, test the compensating controls and decide with your lead
qs.e: Evidence settles classification.

qs.x: What do you do with the junior’s workpaper?
o: Send it back: conclusion must match results; explain and coach
qs.e: An unexplained exception blocks the conclusion.

qs.x: A control is best defined as:
o: A safeguard that reduces the likelihood or impact of something going wrong
qs.e: Controls reduce likelihood or impact.

qs.x: Section 404(b) is performed by:
qs.e: 404(a) is management; 404(b) is the auditor.

qs.x: A monthly manual control typically has a sample size of:
qs.e: Annual 1, quarterly 2, monthly 2 to 5.

qs.x: Which transaction configures posting periods?
qs.e: OB52 is posting periods.

qs.x: A SOC 1 Type II covers:
o: Design and operating effectiveness over a period
qs.e: Type II covers a period.

qs.x: Which test beats SAP’s duplicate invoice check weakness?
o: Fuzzy matching on reference, same amount and vendor within a short window
qs.e: A small change defeats the exact check.

qs.x: Why does the SYSTEM database user matter?
o: Powerful and able to bypass application controls
qs.e: Default SYSTEM must be deactivated or controlled.

qs.x: Which is NOT moved to SAP under RISE?
qs.e: Client keeps user and role administration.

qs.x: What best shows senior ownership in week 1?
o: Confirming scope and timeline in writing and briefing the junior
qs.e: Foundation first.

qs.x: Asked something you do not know, you:
o: State what you know, how you would check, and do not guess
qs.e: Honest reasoning wins.
